blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this paper as a clever method for generating datasets that maintain identical statistical properties while producing visually distinct graphs. The authors, Matejka and Fitzmaurice, demonstrate how simulated annealing can iteratively perturb an initial dataset to achieve target shapes—such as the Datasaurus or Simpson’s paradox examples—without altering key summary statistics. Colyer draws an analogy to adversarial inputs in deep learning, emphasizing how the same statistical outcomes can arise from fundamentally different underlying causes. The paper also explores practical applications like dataset anonymization and showcases the technique’s flexibility across dimensions (1D, 2D, etc.). The core insight is that small, controlled perturbations to data points can systematically reshape visualizations while preserving statistical fidelity, offering a powerful tool for data exploration and privacy-preserving transformations.
paper_title: Same stats, different graphs: generating datasets with varied appearance and identical statistics through simulated annealing
paper_abstract: While summary statistics are used consistently to report data results, their limitations (and the importance of visualizing data) are well known. Yet, current methods that aim to approximate shapes to match some desired summary statistics are quite complex and can fail the approximation for complex shapes. We present a simple linear transformation LT that performs the same approximation more effectively and efficiently. We show that this method works well for complicated shapes and large datasets, visually outperforms almost all baseline algorithms for most shapes, while being significantly faster and simpler. We also present an iterative approach that improves the method LT in case of extreme statistical values.
